summary: Product walkthrough focused on Redwood's structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool calling. Demonstrated console JSON schemas, guardrails, and example tool integrations. Customer requests security docs, pricing, and a POC with perf benchmarks against their QA prompt set.
topics: Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, quant profiles
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood — with me is Lena Ortiz, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:09] Carlos Mendes: Good, thanks. We have about an hour. We're particularly interested in structured output and how function calling could fit into our checkout flows.
[00:18] Lena Ortiz: Great. We built a short demo that shows JSON mode with schemas, plus a function-calling example that emits a validated order object and then triggers a mock 'inventory_check' tool. We'll walk the console and the API path.
[00:30] Priya Raman: Cool. Two quick constraints: we need deterministic schemas for downstream systems, and any PII needs to stay in our VPC. Also latency targets — <150ms for single-turn calls on the checkout path.
[00:42] Jordan Kim: Noted. We'll talk about Dedicated and Private options. For latency, we typically recommend Dedicated pools or private deployment pinned to a GPU profile; Optimize can suggest batching settings for non-critical flows.
[00:56] Evan Lee: On the VPC point, can you do private control plane or do you require a public endpoint?
[01:03] Lena Ortiz: We support private control plane and VPC peering for Private deployments, and Dedicated gives you reserved capacity with VPC egress controls. We'll share diagrams — I know those are important for procurement.
[01:20] Jordan Kim: All right, quick agenda — 1) JSON mode + schemas, 2) function/tool calling, 3) Console walkthrough of guardrails and QA hooks, 4) Optimize recommendations, 5) next steps.
[01:35] [screen share starts] Lena Ortiz: Ok I'm sharing the Console. First, JSON mode — you provide a JSON schema and the model is constrained to output valid JSON that matches the schema. Here is an example checkout schema we use in demos.
[01:50] Lena Ortiz: (reads) "order": {"id": string, "items": [ {"sku": string, "qty": integer } ], "total_cents": integer, "user": {"id": string, "email": string} } — the runtime enforces shape and types, and will surface validation errors in the response.
[02:10] Carlos Mendes: A lot of systems choke on optional fields. Does Redwood support strict vs permissive modes?
[02:16] Lena Ortiz: Yes — strict will reject anything outside the schema; permissive will try to coerce where reasonable and add warnings. We commonly run permissive during ramp, then flip to strict for production.
[02:30] Priya Raman: How does this handle hallucinations where the model invents a field?
[02:37] Lena Ortiz: The JSON mode validator will either drop unexpected fields and add a warning or reject the response depending on the mode. For critical flows we pair this with a short post-validation function that asserts business invariants before committing.
[02:52] [00:03:00] Jordan Kim: Now onto function-calling. We'll show a demo where the model returns a structured order and then the runtime triggers a function — "inventory_check" — which returns stock status.
[03:12] Lena Ortiz: Demo time. (types) API call: model=redwood-rlhf-1, mode=json, schema=checkout_v2.json, tools=[inventory_check].
[03:25] Lena Ortiz: (reads synthesized output) "order": {"id":"ord_9f3","items":[{"sku":"ABC123","qty":2}],"total_cents":5980, ...} — The runtime calls inventory_check with items payload. Inventory responds available:true. The platform can auto-route fallbacks if inventory is down.
[03:45] Evan Lee: Are tool calls synchronous? Can they be async for long-running checks?
[03:50] Lena Ortiz: Both. The runtime supports sync calls with timeouts and async webhooks. For long-running jobs we return a ticket and let the app poll or subscribe to the event via Redwood's callbacks.
[04:05] Carlos Mendes: What's the auth model for tool endpoints?
[04:08] Lena Ortiz: You can use signed tokens (JWT) that Redwood issues per-deployment, mTLS, or short-lived signed URLs. For Private deployments you can also do internal-only endpoints behind your VPC.
[04:22] [00:05:00] Priya Raman: Can you show guardrails at the prompt level — like blocking PII leak or forcing certain enumerations?
[04:30] Jordan Kim: Yep. In the Console we have a Guardrails tab — you can upload blocklists, set regex detectors, and wire evaluation hooks. Here's an example rule that strips credit-card-like strings and flags the result.
[04:49] Lena Ortiz: Also we support content policies that run before and after generation; pre-gen blockers prevent the model from being invoked for risky prompts.
[04:59] Evan Lee: Any chance to see a demo where the model calls a pricing tool and we verify numeric precision?
[05:06] Lena Ortiz: Sure. (types) We'll call pricing_tool(price_matrix_v3) — model returns item prices, we run a pricing function that normalizes to cents and validates rounding. If there's a mismatch the runtime rejects and we can route to a fallback pricing model.
[05:25] [00:08:00] Priya Raman: For our success criteria we need 99.9% schema validity and under 0.1% post-validation exceptions during peak load. Can Redwood hit that?
[05:36] Lena Ortiz: In our Dedicated customers we typically see >99.95% schema conformance once the prompt and schema are tuned. The remaining errors are usually due to prompt edge cases — Optimize can suggest example prompts and quant rules.
[05:50] Jordan Kim: We'll set up a POC with your QA prompt set to measure exactly that.
[05:57] Carlos Mendes: Pricing? If we run high QPS on checkout, what's the recommendation — Dedicated reserved or Hosted with burst?
[06:05] Jordan Kim: For strict latency SLOs, Dedicated reserved capacity is recommended. Hosted is great for ramp and lower-sustained throughput. We can provide cost modeling — Lena has a spreadsheet.
[06:17] Lena Ortiz: I'll share the cost sheet. We also have Optimize suggestions: for checkout we often run int8 quant models with KV cache hot-paths and aggressive prefix caching to keep tails under 150ms.
[06:33] [00:10:00] Evan Lee: Walk me through network egress and KMS integration for tokenization logs. We have strict residency requirements.
[06:42] Lena Ortiz: For Private you control the KMS and logs stay behind your network. For Dedicated we can integrate with customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS/HSM), and we retain audit logs to a customer S3 or your SIEM via syslog. We'll send the security whitepaper.
[06:59] Priya Raman: Can we get a SOC 2 Type II report?
[07:03] Jordan Kim: Yes, we'll include that in the docs pack.
[07:10] [00:12:00] Lena Ortiz: Ok back to the live demo — now I'll show how the Console's Eval hooks work. You can provide golden examples and Redwood will run periodic regression tests and send alerts when exact-match or semantic drift crosses thresholds.
[07:25] Priya Raman: Do you support dataset-level masking so we can send redacted data for evals?
[07:30] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we accept redacted datasets and we also have a built-in data masking tool that will hash or remove PII before storing.
[07:40] Carlos Mendes: Slight tangent — we currently use Anthropic for a couple flows. How hard is model migration?
[07:47] Jordan Kim: We have adapters and a model catalog; most of our customers switch with minimal prompt rework. There are some tokenization and safety differences but our Optimize tooling will recommend prompt and temperature changes.
[07:59] [00:15:00] Lena Ortiz: Demo: function call failure handling. If inventory_check returns error, Redwood can auto-retry, fallback to a cheaper model, or call a queued job. Here, I'll simulate a 500 and show the fallback policy.
[08:18] (demo shows retry -> fallback model returns conservative availability)
[08:26] Evan Lee: For fallbacks, does the platform incur double charges when retrying?
[08:31] Jordan Kim: We meter per invocation; retries count as invocations, but we can cap retries and use cheaper models for fallback to limit cost. Optimize gives recommendations for retry budget vs cost.
[08:45] Priya Raman: How do you handle schema versioning in production? We have breaking changes regularly.
[08:52] Lena Ortiz: The Console has schema versioning with rollout policies — canary, A/B, or gradual percent. You can pin model+schema combos per route. Rollback is immediate if evals spike.
[09:05] [00:18:00] Jordan Kim: Quick Q for you all — what's your expected pilot QPS and typical sequence lengths?
[09:14] Carlos Mendes: Pilot ~200 QPS, average tokens per call ~120, but we have bursts up to 800 QPS.
[09:24] Lena Ortiz: Great — for that footprint we'd recommend a Dedicated pool with burst capacity. Optimize will compute batching windows to keep latency targets.
[09:35] Evan Lee: Are tokenization differences going to affect pricing estimations?
[09:39] Jordan Kim: Somewhat — tokenizers vary but our cost model uses tokens as a unit and we can run sample tokenization on your corpora for accurate estimates.
[09:49] [00:20:00] Priya Raman: Security follow ups — does Redwood support customer-managed encryption keys and HSM?
[09:56] Lena Ortiz: Yes, both supported on Private; Dedicated supports CMK integration for data at rest and in transit. We'll include the HSM options in the packet.
[10:07] Carlos Mendes: Any out-of-the-box monitoring integrations? PagerDuty? Datadog?
[10:12] Lena Ortiz: We integrate with Datadog, Prometheus, PagerDuty, and Splunk. Alerts map to per-route SLAs and trace IDs.
[10:24] [00:22:00] Jordan Kim: I'm going to show one more pattern — structured output with enumerations. If you need strict enums for e.g., payment_method: ["card","apple_pay","paypal"], the validator will enforce that and return a structured error if the model produces something else.
[10:40] Priya Raman: Nice. That covers a lot. Could you also show how we capture the outputs into our event stream?
[10:47] Lena Ortiz: Sure — we have a webhook delivery or direct S3 sink; here's the event envelope — it contains trace_id, validated_payload, model_meta, and any guardrail flags. You can configure encryption for sinks.
[11:05] [00:24:00] (demo pauses; attendees ask clarifying questions)
[11:20] Evan Lee: A small nit — earlier you mentioned KV cash, did you mean KV cache?
[11:24] Lena Ortiz: (laughs) Yes, KV cache — sometimes the transcript thinks I said cash.
[11:30] Jordan Kim: A few pragmatic notes — for POC we'll do: 1) share security pack and pricing, 2) get your redacted prompt set, 3) run benchmark for schema conformance and latency, 4) agree on pilot sizing and T&Cs.
[11:45] Priya Raman: That sounds good. For benchmarks please include 95/99 latency percentiles and schema failure rate.
[11:54] Lena Ortiz: Will do. We'll also include Optimize suggested quant profiles and batching numbers.
[12:05] [00:27:00] Carlos Mendes: Any questions on our side?
[12:08] Priya Raman: One — for offline reconciliation, can the model output justification snippets that tie to prompt text? We want auditability.
[12:15] Lena Ortiz: Yes. The runtime can include token-level highlights and rationale fields, but note that increases token counts; we can sample for audit logs to save cost.
[12:29] Evan Lee: For the pilot, we'll likely want dedicated capacity in a single region near our users. Can you support region restrictions?
[12:35] Jordan Kim: Yes — we have region pinning and can provision Dedicated pools in multiple cloud regions.
[12:43] [00:30:00] (demo wraps up; screen share off)
[12:50] Jordan Kim: Quick recap — we showed JSON mode + schema enforcement, function/tool calling patterns, guardrails and evals, and deployment/security options. Next steps: Lena will send the cost sheet + demo notebooks, Jordan will send security docs and POC proposal.
[13:10] Priya Raman: We'll share a redacted QA set and success criteria by Monday.
[13:18] Carlos Mendes: And procurement will need SOC2 and an MSA draft.
[13:24] Jordan Kim: We'll include standard MSA and SOW templates.
[13:30] [00:33:00] (some side chatter about internal scheduling)
[13:50] Evan Lee: One last technical — do you expose KV cache metrics per-route so we can monitor cache hit rates?
[13:57] Lena Ortiz: Yep, per-route telemetry includes cache hits, token breakdowns, and cost per-token; you can set alerts on cache hit degradation.
[14:10] Priya Raman: Great. Any other blockers?
[14:12] Carlos Mendes: Not right now.
[14:18] Jordan Kim: Awesome — we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the POC kickoff. Thanks everyone.
[14:26] Priya Raman: Thanks, bye.
[14:28] Evan Lee: Bye.
[14:30] Lena Ortiz: Thanks all, bye.
[57:55] [call end]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cash" instead of KV cache), short crosstalk, and some filler words removed for readability.
